sections.title: What an Animal Bought with *Shevi'it* Produce Can Be Used For
sections.gist: *Shevi'it* produce is given for eating, not for trade or burning. So a lamb bought with it may not redeem a certain *peter chamor*, though Rav Chisda allows a doubtful one. Its own firstborn is not a *bekhor*, though the animal owes *matnot kehunah*, a line the Gemara tests against *challah*.

children.title: Can a *Shevi'it* Lamb Redeem a Doubtful *Peter Chamor*?
children.gist: Handing a *shevi'it* lamb to a kohen in exchange for a donkey is trade, so a certain *peter chamor* can't be redeemed with it. Rav Chisda rules that a doubtful one can, since there the owner keeps the lamb and eats it.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks whether a *peter chamor* (firstborn donkey) may be redeemed with a lamb bought with *shevi'it* produce. The purchase carries *kedushat shevi'it* (the sanctity of Sabbatical-year produce) over to the lamb.
For a certain *peter chamor* the answer is plainly no. The owner gives the lamb to the kohen and gets his donkey free in return, and *shevi'it* produce is “for eating” (Vayikra 25:6), not for trade.

So the question is only about a doubtful *peter chamor*, and only by R. Yehuda, who requires the owner to designate a lamb to lift the donkey's prohibition and lets him keep it. R. Shimon holds a doubtful one needs no redemption at all, so for him the question never arises.

Two ways to see it. The lamb stays the owner's and he eats it, so it is still used “for eating”. Or, since the donkey stays forbidden until the lamb frees it, using the lamb to free it is itself a kind of trade.
Rav Chisda settles it: a *shevi'it* animal may not redeem a certain *peter chamor*, but it may redeem a doubtful one.
The line falls at handing the lamb over. As long as it never goes to the kohen, nothing has been exchanged, and the lamb is simply eaten.

children.title: Rav Chisda: A *Shevi'it* Animal's Firstborn Isn't Holy, but It Owes *Matnot Kehunah*
children.gist: Rav Chisda rules that an animal bought with *shevi'it* produce is exempt from *bekhorah* but owes *matnot kehunah*. A *bekhor* is partly burned on the altar, while the gifts are eaten by the kohen.

bullets.text: Rav Chisda: an animal bought with *shevi'it* produce is exempt from *bekhorah* (the sanctity of a firstborn), yet owes *matnot kehunah* (the gifts a kohen receives when an ordinary animal is slaughtered).

The reason: the Torah gave *shevi'it* produce “for eating”, not for burning, and parts of a kosher *bekhor* are burned on the altar. The gifts, by contrast, are eaten by the kohen, so they count as “for eating”.
A *bekhor* is by its nature an offering whose innards go on the altar, so it clashes with a sanctity that demands the animal be eaten.

children.title: Why *Shevi'it* Dough Owes Challah, Though Its Animal's Firstborn Is Exempt
children.gist: A Mishnah holds *shevi'it* dough liable for *challah*, though *challah* that becomes impure is burned. The Gemara grounds this in “throughout your generations”, and explains why the *bekhor* can't follow: *challah* is mainly eaten, while the *bekhor*'s altar portions are mainly burned.

bullets.text: Objection from a Mishnah (Shevi'it 9:9): one who eats *shevi'it* dough before its *challah* (the portion of dough given to a kohen) is separated incurs death at the hands of Heaven. So *shevi'it* dough owes *challah*.
Yet *challah* that becomes impure must be burned. By Rav Chisda's logic, “for eating, not for burning” should exempt *shevi'it* dough, just as it exempts the *shevi'it* animal's firstborn.

Answer: *challah* has its own verse, “throughout your generations” (Bamidbar 15:21), which takes in the Sabbatical year too. A baraita derives the same and notes that no such phrase is written of the *bekhor*.
Why not learn the *bekhor* from *challah*? Dough is meant mainly for eating and is burned only if it becomes impure, while the altar portions of a *bekhor* are meant for burning.
Burning is a contingency for *challah* but the core act of a *bekhor*, so only the *bekhor* truly clashes with *kedushat shevi'it*.

sections.title: Why Every Kohen Is Suspect of Using an Unredeemed *Peter Chamor*
sections.gist: A baraita forbids handing a *peter chamor* to a kohen who promises to redeem it, unless he redeems it in the owner's presence. Rav Nachman draws the rule that every kohen is suspect, since he can tell himself the lamb will be his anyway.

bullets.text: The Mishnah had a kohen keep a donated *peter chamor* only after redeeming it. A baraita spells it out: if a kohen says “Give it to me and I will redeem it”, the owner may not hand it over unless the kohen redeems it in his presence.
Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh: this shows that kohanim are suspect of using a *peter chamor* without redeeming it.

Isn't that obvious from the baraita? Not quite: one might have limited it to a kohen known to have done this before. Rav Nachman teaches that it applies to every kohen, since he may permit himself the donkey, reasoning that the lamb would end up his anyway.
The kohen is both the one who redeems and the one who receives, so the redemption looks to him like a formality, and he treats it as already done.

An acharon notes that the Torah never entitles the kohen to the donkey itself, only to a lamb: a donkey that dies can't be given to him at all. How handing over the donkey fulfills the mitzvah remains an open question.

sections.title: When the Redemption of a *Peter Chamor* Takes Effect
sections.gist: R. Eliezer holds the owner bears *achrayut* for the designated lamb until the kohen receives it, as with a firstborn son's 5 *sela'im*; the Rabbis hold the donkey is redeemed once the lamb is designated, as with *ma'aser sheni* money. The Gemara then asks how far R. Eliezer compares the donkey to a firstborn son.

children.title: Mishnah: The Designated Lamb Dies, or the Donkey Dies
children.gist: If the designated lamb dies, R. Eliezer makes the owner replace it and the Rabbis don't. If the donkey dies instead, R. Eliezer has it buried and lets the owner keep the lamb, while the Rabbis need no burial and give the lamb to the kohen.

bullets.text: Mishnah (R. Eliezer): if the lamb designated for a *peter chamor* dies, the owner bears *achrayut* (financial responsibility for it) and must give another, like a firstborn son's 5 *sela'im* lost before reaching the kohen.
Mishnah (the Rabbis): he bears no responsibility, like money designated to redeem *ma'aser sheni* (second-tithe produce), which frees the produce the moment it is designated.
R. Yehoshua and R. Tzadok testify that when the designated lamb died, “the kohen has nothing here”, in line with the Rabbis.
If the donkey died after the lamb was designated, R. Eliezer: the donkey is buried, and the owner may benefit from the lamb. The Rabbis: it needs no burial, and the lamb is given to the kohen.

Each side is consistent. For R. Eliezer nothing is redeemed until the lamb is handed over, so the dead donkey was never redeemed and stays forbidden, and there is nothing left to redeem. For the Rabbis the donkey was already redeemed, so it is permitted and the lamb is owed.
Tosafot: since we follow the Rabbis, the *berakhah* on redeeming a *peter chamor* is said at designating the lamb, unlike *pidyon ha'ben*, where it is said on handing over the money.

children.title: How Far R. Eliezer Compares a *Peter Chamor* to a Firstborn Son
children.gist: Rav Yosef bases R. Eliezer on Bamidbar 18:15, which sets the firstborn son beside the *peter chamor*. Abaye objects that an unredeemed son may be used, while R. Eliezer forbids the donkey; Rava answers that the verse compares them only regarding redemption.

bullets.text: Rav Yosef: “you shall redeem the firstborn of man, and the firstborn of non-kosher animals you shall redeem” (Bamidbar 18:15) compares the two. As a father bears *achrayut* for the 5 *sela'im* until they are given, the owner bears it for the lamb.

Abaye: then, like a firstborn son, an unredeemed *peter chamor* should be permitted in benefit, for shearing and work. Yet R. Eliezer requires a dead donkey to be buried, which can only mean that benefit is forbidden.
Rav Yosef: it is buried as a firstborn son is buried. The Gemara dismisses this: every person is buried, firstborn or not, so the comparison can't produce a burial rule.

Further, a baraita: R. Eliezer concedes that for a doubtful *peter chamor* the owner designates a lamb and keeps it. That lamb serves only to lift the ban on benefit, so R. Eliezer plainly holds the donkey forbidden.
Rava: the doubled verb *pado tifdeh* limits the comparison to redemption, the *achrayut* for the lamb, and not to any other matter, such as benefit from the animal.
The doubtful case also shows when R. Eliezer requires handing over: where the lamb never has to reach a kohen, designating it is enough even for him.

sections.title: When the Obligation to Redeem a *Peter Chamor* Begins
sections.gist: One baraita says a *peter chamor* is redeemed immediately, another that it has nothing under 30 days. Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet each try to reconcile them, and Rava ties them to R. Eliezer vs. the Rabbis.

children.title: Rav Nachman: “Immediately” Means Valid After the Fact
children.gist: One baraita redeems a *peter chamor* immediately, another sets 30 days as its minimum. Rav Nachman reads “immediately” as valid after the fact, and the Gemara checks this against Rav's ruling on a son redeemed early.

bullets.text: Baraita: valuations are fixed by the time of the vow; a firstborn son is redeemed after 30 days, “from a month old shall you redeem them” (Bamidbar 18:16); a *peter chamor*, immediately.
A second baraita: valuations, a firstborn son, *nezirut* and a *peter chamor* have nothing under 30 days, though they extend without limit. So the donkey too waits 30 days.
Rav Nachman: “immediately” means that if he redeemed it at once, it is redeemed, though the proper time is after 30 days.

By that inference a son redeemed early would not be redeemed, yet Rav ruled that he is. Rava explains Rav: all agree that redeeming “from now” fails; Rav means money given now on condition that the redemption take effect at 30 days.
So a son can't be redeemed before 30 days even after the fact, while a donkey can.

children.title: Rav Sheshet: The Mitzvah Starts at Birth, the Transgression After 30 Days
children.gist: Rav Sheshet holds the mitzvah applies from birth, and 30 days marks only when delay becomes a transgression. Rami bar Chama objects from a baraita that leaves a fresh choice after 30 days, to redeem or perform *arifah*.

bullets.text: Rav Sheshet: the mitzvah takes effect at birth, as the first baraita says. “Not under 30 days” means that until then a delay is no transgression; after 30 days it is.

Rami bar Chama objects from a baraita: the mitzvah applies throughout 30 days, and from then on he either redeems it or performs *arifah* (breaking its neck). Doesn't that mean a mitzvah to wait the 30 days?

The Gemara tries: it means a mitzvah to redeem within 30 days, after which he transgresses. But then the baraita should say “redeems it or transgresses”, not offer the choice of redeeming or *arifah*.

children.title: Rava: One Baraita Follows R. Eliezer, the Other the Rabbis
children.gist: Rava resolves the contradiction. The 30-day baraita follows R. Eliezer, who compares the *peter chamor* to a firstborn son; the “immediately” baraita follows the Rabbis, who don't.

bullets.text: Rava: the baraita that waits 30 days is R. Eliezer's, who compares the donkey to a firstborn son, of whom it says “from a month old shall you redeem them”. The one requiring immediate redemption is the Rabbis', who make no comparison.
This joins the timing question to the Mishnah's dispute: whoever treats the redemption like a son's, complete only on handing over, also takes on the son's 30 days.

Rambam rules with the Rabbis: the mitzvah starts at birth. After 30 days the owner should decide, and further delay postpones a mitzvah, but it is no Torah transgression, since without the comparison 30 days has no source.
Some acharonim note that the Gemara speaks of transgressing after 30 days; for Rambam that language belongs to Rav Sheshet, not to the conclusion.

returns_to.note: Ties the timing to R. Eliezer's comparison of the *peter chamor* to a firstborn son

sections.title: Mishnah: Redemption Before *Arifah*, and Other Mitzvot That Take Precedence
sections.gist: If the owner won't redeem the *peter chamor*, he performs *arifah* and buries it, but redemption comes first. The Mishnah adds three more pairs: *yi'ud* before redeeming a Hebrew maidservant, *yibum* before *chalitzah* (later reversed), and the owner's redemption of *hekdesh* before anyone else's.

bullets.text: Mishnah: if he does not wish to redeem the donkey, he performs *arifah* from behind and buries it. Redemption takes precedence: “If you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck” (Shemot 13:13).

It is buried because a *peter chamor* is forbidden in benefit. Rambam counts *arifah* as a mitzvah of its own, since the Mishnah calls it “the mitzvah of *arifah*”; the Ra'avad objects that it is only what one does after failing the real mitzvah. Some answer that a mitzvah can set the procedure for a choice that isn't ideal, like divorce.
*Yi'ud* (the master designating a Hebrew maidservant as his wife) precedes her redemption: “who has not designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed” (Shemot 21:8).

*Yibum* (levirate marriage) precedes *chalitzah* (the ceremony that releases the widow): “And if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife” (Devarim 25:7). That held while men intended the mitzvah; once they married for beauty or money, the Sages said *chalitzah* comes first.
The Gemara in Yevamot suggests that *yibum* without the right intent borders on a forbidden relationship. Sefardim still rule that *yibum* comes first.

A non-kosher animal consecrated to *hekdesh* (the Temple treasury) is redeemed first by its owner, before anyone else: “and if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold according to your valuation” (Vayikra 27:27).
The Temple gains by this, since an owner who redeems adds a fifth to the price.

sections.title: Mishnah: A Gentile's Share Exempts the Firstborn, but Kohanim and Levi'im Are Obligated
sections.gist: If a gentile owns any share of the mother or the offspring, the firstborn is not a *bekhor*, since the Torah sanctified the firstborn “in Israel”. Kohanim and Levi'im, exempt from redeeming a son or a *peter chamor*, are still bound by *bekhorah*.

bullets.text: Mishnah: five cases are exempt: buying the fetus of a gentile's cow; selling one's cow's fetus to a gentile (though selling him a large animal is forbidden); a partnership with a gentile; taking a gentile's cow to raise for a share of its young; or giving one's cow to a gentile on those terms.
The source: “I sanctified to Me all the firstborn in Israel, both man and animal” (Bamidbar 3:13). The sanctity falls on Israel and not on others, so even a partial gentile share removes it.
Kohanim and Levi'im are obligated in the firstborn of a kosher animal. They were exempted only from redeeming a firstborn son and a *peter chamor*.

Their exemption comes from the exchange in the wilderness, when the Levi'im and their animals took the place of Israel's firstborn. That covers the mitzvot of redemption, not a kosher firstborn's own sanctity as an offering.

sections.title: Why the Tractate Opens with the Donkey Rather Than the Cow
sections.gist: Why does the tractate begin with the *peter chamor*, whose sanctity rests only in its value, rather than the kosher firstborn, which is holy in itself? Two answers from Eretz Yisrael: the donkey's laws are dear, and they are few.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks: the kosher firstborn has *kedushat haguf* (inherent sanctity) and is offered on the altar, while the *peter chamor*'s sanctity rests in its value. Shouldn't the weightier case come first?
In Eretz Yisrael they answered: the donkey's laws are dear, since donkeys carried Israel's gold and silver out of Egypt.
Or: the laws of a non-kosher animal are few, so the *tanna* finishes them first and sets them aside.

sections.title: Acquiring from a Gentile by *Kesef* or by *Meshikhah*
sections.gist: R. Oshaya's baraita rules that *kesef* alone moves an animal between a Jew and a gentile in either direction, which Abaye reads from “from your counterpart's hand”. Ameimar holds *meshikhah* acquires from a gentile, and the Gemara works out how that fits R. Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish on how Jews acquire by Torah law.

children.title: R. Oshaya: *Kesef* Acquires Between a Jew and a Gentile
children.gist: R. Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports, from Reish Lakish in the name of R. Oshaya, that payment “according to their laws” acquires without *meshikhah* in both directions. A Jew who buys becomes liable for the firstborn; a Jew who sells is freed of it.

bullets.text: A Jew who gave money for a gentile's animal “according to their laws” acquires it even without *meshikhah* (pulling the animal, the act that ordinarily acquires movables). So he is obligated to give its firstborn to a kohen.

A gentile who paid a Jew for his animal likewise acquires it without pulling, so the Jew is exempt from its firstborn. In both directions it is *kesef* (payment as the act of acquisition) that transfers ownership.

The question carries weight in practice: for selling a share of an animal to a gentile to exempt its firstborn, for selling *chametz*, and for *heter mekhirah* (selling land to a gentile for the Sabbatical year).

children.title: How a Jew Acquires a Gentile's Animal
children.gist: What does “according to their laws” mean? The Gemara rejects an inference from buying a gentile slave, and Abaye reads it as the Torah's own rule for a gentile, drawn from “from your counterpart's hand”.

children.title: The Gemara Rejects Learning from the Purchase of a Gentile Slave
children.gist: One might reason that since a gentile slave is acquired with money, his property surely is. The Gemara rejects it: that would let a document or *chazakah* acquire too, and a Jewish slave is bought with money though a Jew's goods need pulling.

bullets.text: Proposal: “their laws” are the laws of buying a gentile's person. A Canaanite slave is compared to an ancestral holding (Vayikra 25:46), and land is acquired by money, a document or *chazakah* (taking possession), so a slave is acquired by money, and his property all the more.
Rejected: by that logic a gentile's property could also be acquired by a document or by *chazakah*, which it can't.
And a Jew disproves the inference: his person, as a Hebrew slave, is bought with money, yet his goods only by pulling. How a person is acquired says nothing about his property.

children.title: Abaye Derives *Kesef* from “Your Counterpart's Hand”
children.gist: Abaye: “their laws” are the ones the Torah set for gentiles. “From your counterpart's hand” makes *meshikhah* the mode with a Jew, so *kesef* is the mode with a gentile, and the Gemara rules out three other readings.

bullets.text: Abaye: “or buy from your counterpart's hand” (Vayikra 25:14). A hand passes the object over, so from a Jew one acquires by *meshikhah*; from a gentile, by *kesef*.
Tosafot: a sale has two acts, paying and taking the object. If the verse gives one to the Jew, the other is left for the gentile.
Perhaps nothing can be bought from a gentile at all? No: if his very person can be bought, surely his property can.
Perhaps both acts are needed with a gentile? No: his person is acquired by one act, so his property can't need two.
Perhaps either act works? No: the gentile's case mirrors “your counterpart”, where a single act acquires, so with a gentile *kesef* alone.

children.title: How a Gentile Acquires a Jew's Animal
children.gist: The same reasoning runs in reverse when a gentile buys from a Jew. The slave inference fails again, and Abaye reads “if you sell to your counterpart” to make *kesef* the gentile's mode of acquisition.

bullets.text: Proposal: a gentile buys a Hebrew slave with money, “from the money of his purchase” (Vayikra 25:51), so surely he can buy a Jew's goods that way. Rejected, since a Jew buys a Hebrew slave with money but a Jew's goods only by pulling.
Abaye: “and if you sell a sale item to your counterpart” (Vayikra 25:14). Selling to a Jew is by *meshikhah*, so selling to a gentile is by *kesef*.

The three alternatives fall as before: a gentile can buy a Jew's person, so he can buy his goods; one act for the person can't mean two for property; and, as with “your counterpart”, a single act acquires.

children.title: Ameimar: *Meshikhah* Acquires from a Gentile
children.gist: Ameimar holds *meshikhah* acquires in dealings with a gentile. The Gemara shows this fits R. Yochanan, for whom *kesef* acquires between Jews by Torah law, and asks what “your counterpart” would teach if Ameimar followed Reish Lakish.

children.title: Ameimar's View Under R. Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish
children.gist: If Ameimar follows R. Yochanan, “your counterpart” teaches that Jews acquire by *kesef* and a gentile by *meshikhah*. If he follows Reish Lakish, both acquire by *meshikhah*, and the phrase seems to teach nothing.

bullets.text: Ameimar: *meshikhah* acquires in the case of a gentile.

That works by R. Yochanan, who holds that by Torah law *kesef* acquires and pulling does not. Then “your counterpart” contrasts Jews, who acquire by *kesef*, with a gentile, who acquires by *meshikhah*.

The Sages later required pulling between Jews too, lest goods paid for be lost while still with the seller. So in practice both acquire by *meshikhah*, Jews by rabbinic enactment and gentiles by Torah law.
By Reish Lakish, *meshikhah* is explicit in the Torah, so Jews and gentiles alike would acquire by pulling. Why, then, does the verse say “your counterpart”?

children.title: “Your Counterpart” Teaches No *Ona'ah* Toward a Gentile or *Hekdesh*
children.gist: The Gemara suggests “your counterpart” teaches that *ona'ah* isn't returned to a gentile. Since “a man shall not exploit his brother” already excludes him, the two phrases are split: one excludes a gentile, the other *hekdesh*.

bullets.text: Proposal: the phrase serves the end of the verse, “a man shall not exploit his brother” (Vayikra 25:14). One returns *ona'ah* (overcharging) to a fellow Jew, but not to a gentile.
Objection: “his brother” already excludes a gentile, so “your counterpart” is still extra.
Answer: one phrase excludes a gentile and the other *hekdesh*. Both are needed, since from one alone we might have exempted the gentile but still applied *ona'ah* to *hekdesh*.
Many rishonim held that such distinctions don't apply to gentiles who live by law, and the conclusion in Bava Kamma is that robbing a gentile is forbidden.

children.title: If Robbing a Gentile Is Permitted, Ameimar Must Follow R. Yochanan
children.gist: The *ona'ah* answer works only if robbing a gentile is forbidden; if it is permitted, overcharging him needs no verse. So if Ameimar holds that robbing a gentile is permitted, he must follow R. Yochanan.

bullets.text: The *ona'ah* reading works for one who holds robbing a gentile forbidden: then a verse is needed to let one keep an overcharge from him.
But if robbing him is permitted, keeping an overcharge surely is, and the verse would teach nothing.
The Sages conclude: if Ameimar holds that robbing a gentile is permitted, he perforce follows R. Yochanan, so “your counterpart” contrasts *kesef* with *meshikhah* and the difficulty doesn't arise.
In practice the poskim follow Ameimar that *meshikhah* acquires from a gentile, and many advise doing both *kinyan kesef* and *meshikhah* when selling to a gentile.

key_terms.definition: The firstborn male of a donkey. It is forbidden in benefit until its owner redeems it with a lamb given to a kohen; if he will not redeem it, he must break its neck.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks what may redeem it, when the redemption takes effect (R. Eliezer vs. the Rabbis), and whether it is redeemed at once or after 30 days.

key_terms.definition: The sanctity of produce grown in the Sabbatical year, which must be used for eating and not for trade or destruction; the sanctity passes to whatever is bought with it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Because such produce is “for eating, not for burning” or trade, an animal bought with it can't redeem a certain *peter chamor* and its firstborn is not a *bekhor*.

key_terms.sense: gifts from a slaughtered animal to a kohen
key_terms.definition: The foreleg, jaw and maw that must be given to a kohen from every non-sacred kosher animal that is slaughtered.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Chisda rules that an animal bought with *shevi'it* produce owes them, since the kohen eats them.

key_terms.sense: liability for a designated item until delivered
key_terms.definition: An owner's financial responsibility for something he has set aside for another, so that if it is lost or dies he must replace it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Eliezer makes the owner liable for the lamb designated for a *peter chamor* until the kohen receives it; the Rabbis don't.

key_terms.sense: breaking the neck of an unredeemed peter chamor
key_terms.definition: Killing a firstborn donkey by breaking its neck from behind, done when its owner chooses not to redeem it; the carcass is buried.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah rules that redemption takes precedence over *arifah*, and a baraita leaves the owner a choice between them after 30 days.

key_terms.definition: Acquiring a movable object, such as an animal, by pulling it toward oneself; the standard act of acquisition for movables.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Oshaya's baraita makes it the mode between Jews only; Ameimar makes it the mode in dealings with a gentile.

key_terms.definition: Acquiring by handing over payment, the act that acquires land and, according to some views, movables by Torah law.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Oshaya's baraita has payment alone transfer an animal between a Jew and a gentile; R. Yochanan holds it is the Torah's mode between Jews.

key_terms.definition: Charging more, or paying less, than an item's market value beyond the permitted margin; the excess must be returned or the sale may be voided.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara derives that *ona'ah* is not returned to a gentile, nor in dealings with *hekdesh*.

quiz.q: A man has a doubtful *peter chamor* and, following R. Yehuda, wants to designate a lamb bought with *shevi'it* produce and keep it. What does Rav Chisda rule?
options: Permitted, since the lamb stays his and is eaten, so nothing is traded
Forbidden, since lifting the donkey's prohibition is a kind of trade
Permitted only if he then gives the lamb to a kohen
Forbidden, since *shevi'it* produce may never be used for a mitzvah
quiz.why: Only handing the lamb to a kohen in exchange for the donkey looks like trade; a lamb the owner keeps and eats is still used “for eating”.

quiz.q: An animal bought with *shevi'it* produce gives birth to a firstborn, and is later slaughtered. Why does Rav Chisda exempt the firstborn from *bekhorah* but require *matnot kehunah*?
options: *Shevi'it* produce is for eating, not burning: a *bekhor* is partly burned on the altar, while the gifts are eaten by the kohen
The firstborn belongs to the public, since *shevi'it* produce is ownerless
The gifts are rabbinic, so *shevi'it* doesn't affect them
A *bekhor* can't be sold, and *shevi'it* produce must be traded
quiz.why: “For eating, not for burning”: the *bekhor*'s altar portions are burned, but the kohen eats the gifts.

quiz.q: *Challah* that becomes impure must be burned. Why, then, is *shevi'it* dough still liable for *challah*, unlike the firstborn of a *shevi'it* animal?
options: Dough is mainly for eating and burned only if it becomes impure, and “throughout your generations” includes the Sabbatical year
*Challah* is only rabbinic
*Shevi'it* sanctity doesn't apply to grain
The kohen burns *challah* in any case
quiz.why: Burning is a rare contingency for *challah* but the essential act for a *bekhor*'s altar portions, and *challah* has its own inclusive verse.

quiz.q: A kohen tells an Israelite, “Give me your *peter chamor* and I will redeem it.” He has no record of misusing such donkeys. What is the rule?
options: He may not hand it over unless the kohen redeems it in his presence, since any kohen may tell himself the lamb is his anyway
He may hand it over, since only a kohen known to misuse donkeys is suspect
He may hand it over if the kohen swears to redeem it
He may never give a *peter chamor* to a kohen
quiz.why: Rav Nachman: every kohen is suspect, because the lamb would end up his, so he may treat the redemption as a formality.

quiz.q: A man designates a lamb to redeem his *peter chamor*, and the lamb dies before reaching the kohen. What do the Rabbis rule?
options: He owes nothing: the donkey was redeemed at designation, like money for *ma'aser sheni*
He must give another lamb, like a firstborn son's five *sela'im*
He must break the donkey's neck
He must give the kohen the donkey instead
quiz.why: For the Rabbis the redemption takes effect the moment the lamb is designated, so its loss falls on the kohen; R. Eliezer makes the owner replace it.

quiz.q: One baraita redeems a *peter chamor* immediately, another not under thirty days. How does Rava reconcile them?
options: The thirty-day baraita follows R. Eliezer, who compares it to a firstborn son; the other follows the Rabbis, who don't
Thirty days is the ideal; earlier is valid after the fact
The mitzvah starts at birth, but delay becomes a transgression only after thirty days
One speaks of a certain *peter chamor*, the other of a doubtful one
quiz.why: Whoever compares the donkey to a firstborn son also takes on the son's “from a month old”; the Rabbis, who don't compare, require redemption at once.

quiz.q: A Jew sells the fetus of his cow to a gentile, and it is born a firstborn male. What is its status?
options: Not a *bekhor*: a gentile's share in the offspring removes the sanctity
A *bekhor*, since the mother is the Jew's
A *bekhor* given to a kohen in partnership with the gentile
A *bekhor* only if the gentile owns less than half
quiz.why: “I sanctified to Me all the firstborn in Israel”: even a partial gentile share in the mother or offspring exempts it.

quiz.q: A Jew paid a gentile for his animal but has not yet pulled it. According to R. Oshaya's baraita, does the Jew own it?
options: Yes: from a gentile, *kesef* alone acquires, so its firstborn is holy
No: only *meshikhah* acquires from a gentile
No: he needs both *kesef* and *meshikhah*
Only if the gentile agreed to Jewish law
quiz.why: Abaye reads “from your counterpart's hand”: from a Jew by *meshikhah*, so from a gentile by *kesef*. Ameimar disagrees and requires *meshikhah*.

judgment_calls: The timing question (12b.23–13a.3) is a top-level section rather than a third child of the R. Eliezer vs. Rabbis dispute: the Gemara opens it from an unrelated baraita and only Rava's last step ties it back, so it is linked with returns_to instead.

Line 13a.3 holds both the end of the objection to Rav Sheshet and Rava's resolution; the Rav Sheshet section runs through 13a.3 and Rava's section is anchored to 13a.3 alone, so the two overlap by one line.
The four precedence rulings of 13a.4–7 are kept as one Mishnah section with a chart rather than split, since they are a single list built on one pattern.

The question of why the tractate opens with the donkey (13a.11–12) is a top-level section of its own rather than a child of the Mishnah on gentile ownership; it concerns the order of the tractate, not that Mishnah's content.
Ameimar's discussion (13b.2–6) is nested under the acquisition section with three children, since its *ona'ah* and robbery steps serve only to test whether his view fits R. Yochanan or Reish Lakish.

daf_summary.summary: Discussion of: what an animal bought with *shevi'it* produce may be used for (redeeming a *peter chamor*, *bekhorah*, *matnot kehunah*, and *challah*); why a kohen may not take a *peter chamor* on his promise to redeem it; when the redemption takes effect, and when the obligation to redeem begins; the Mishnah's mitzvot that take precedence, and its cases where a gentile's share exempts the firstborn; and whether *kesef* or *meshikhah* acquires between a Jew and a gentile.

takeaways.text: *Shevi'it* produce is given for eating, not for trade or burning. A lamb bought with it may not redeem a certain *peter chamor*, and its own firstborn is not a *bekhor*, yet it owes *matnot kehunah*, which the kohen eats.
A kohen may not take a *peter chamor* on his promise to redeem it, since any kohen may tell himself the lamb would be his anyway. He must redeem it in the owner's presence.

For R. Eliezer the redemption is complete only when the lamb reaches the kohen, as with a firstborn son; for the Rabbis, once the lamb is designated. Rava ties the two baraitot on timing to the same dispute: waiting 30 days follows R. Eliezer's comparison, redeeming immediately follows the Rabbis.
Any gentile share in the mother or the offspring exempts the firstborn, while kohanim and Levi'im remain bound by *bekhorah*.

Between a Jew and a gentile, R. Oshaya's baraita has *kesef* alone acquire, read from “your counterpart's hand”; Ameimar has *meshikhah* acquire, which fits R. Yochanan's view that between Jews *kesef* acquires by Torah law.

debates.question: When is a *peter chamor* redeemed: when the lamb is designated, or when it reaches the kohen?

sides.view: When it reaches the kohen: a lamb that dies must be replaced, and a donkey that dies is buried

sides.who: The Rabbis, with R. Yehoshua and R. Tzadok
sides.view: When it is designated: a lamb that dies needn't be replaced, and if the donkey dies the lamb goes to the kohen

debates.outcome: The halakha follows the Rabbis, so the *berakhah* is said on designating the lamb (Tosafot).

debates.question: When does the obligation to redeem a *peter chamor* begin?

sides.view: Redeeming at once is valid after the fact; the proper time is after 30 days
The mitzvah starts at birth; only after 30 days is delay a transgression
The 30-day baraita follows R. Eliezer, the “immediately” baraita the Rabbis

debates.outcome: Rambam rules with the Rabbis: the mitzvah starts at birth.

debates.question: Which act acquires an animal between a Jew and a gentile?
debates.outcome: If Ameimar holds that robbing a gentile is permitted, he must follow R. Yochanan; the poskim follow Ameimar, and many advise doing both.
